title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
bodyMarkdown:
# Infrastructure as Code with Terraform

**Infrastructure as Code (IaC)** means provisioning cloud resources from declarative configuration kept in version control. Google's own guidance calls [Terraform](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/terraform-overview) "the most commonly used tool to provision and automate Google Cloud infrastructure," and the exam treats it as the default IaC answer. Expect questions on four things: where state lives and how it is locked, how code is structured for reuse across environments, how automation authenticates, and where managed alternatives (Infrastructure Manager, Config Connector) fit.

## Why IaC and what Terraform gives you

Terraform lets you declare the end state, generate an execution plan, and apply it. That gives you:

- **Reproducibility**: the same configuration deployed multiple times yields consistent dev, test, and production environments.
- **Predictability**: `terraform plan` shows what will change before anything does, so reviewers see a diff, not a surprise.
- **Reuse**: modules package common resource groups behind a standard interface; Google publishes opinionated modules as blueprints and Jump Start Solutions.
- **Auditability and recovery**: changes flow through Git pull requests, and an environment can be rebuilt from code after an incident.

How it works: you describe infrastructure in configuration files; `terraform plan` evaluates them against state and produces a plan; `terraform apply` calls Google Cloud APIs and updates the **state file**, a JSON mapping of configuration to real-world resources. On the next run Terraform compares code, state, and reality: resources in config but not state are created, differing resources are updated, and resources removed from config are destroyed.

## Core building blocks

| Concept | What it is | Exam angle |
|---|---|---|
| Provider | Plugin that talks to an API (`google`, `google-beta`) | Pin versions for deterministic runs |
| Resource | A declared object, for example `google_storage_bucket` | Declarative, not scripted |
| Variable and output | Inputs and exposed results | Outputs are how root modules share values |
| Module | Reusable, parameterized resource group | Answer to "reuse across environments" |
| State | Mapping from config to real resources | Remote, locked, versioned, segmented |
| Backend | Where state is stored (for example `gcs`) | Cloud Storage for teams and CI |

## State management

By default, Terraform [stores state locally](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/resource-management/store-state) in `terraform.tfstate`. Google notes this "can make Terraform usage difficult for teams when multiple users run Terraform at the same time and each machine has its own understanding of the current infrastructure." The fix is a **remote backend in a Cloud Storage bucket**.

Facts to know:

- The `gcs` backend [supports state locking](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/backend/gcs), which stops two simultaneous `apply` runs from corrupting state. Locking is what answers "two engineers applied at once and the state broke."
- The bucket must exist before you configure the backend, which is why Google's tutorial first creates it with local state and then migrates.
- Turn on **Object Versioning** so earlier state versions survive deletion or mistakes. Google's tutorial bucket also sets `public_access_prevention = "enforced"`, `uniform_bucket_level_access = true`, and `force_destroy = false`. Versioning adds storage cost; mitigate it with Object Lifecycle Management that deletes old state versions.
- **Never commit `terraform.tfstate` to Git.** It can hold sensitive values in plaintext and Git offers no locking or merge semantics for it.
- Restrict bucket access with IAM; state is sensitive data.

## Structuring code for environments

Google's [root module guidance](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/root-modules) is specific and testable:

- **Keep state small**: do not include more than 100 resources in a single state, and ideally only a few dozen, because every resource is refreshed on every run.
- **One directory per application or service** (for example shared networking is its own service), so teams change them independently.
- **Split `modules/` from `environments/`**: a `modules/<service>` directory holds the reusable configuration; `environments/dev`, `qa`, and `prod` each hold a `backend.tf` (state location, typically Cloud Storage) and a `main.tf` that instantiates the service module.
- **Use only the default workspace** per environment directory. Multiple CLI workspaces behind one backend are discouraged: configurations are hard to inspect, the shared backend becomes a single point of failure, and conditional logic on `terraform.workspace` hurts readability. Separate directories and separate state per environment is the recommended pattern.
- **Expose outputs through remote state**: other configurations read root-module outputs through `terraform_remote_state`.
- **Pin to minor provider versions** (for example `~> 4.0.0`) to take patch releases but keep a stable target, and name the file `versions.tf`.
- **Provide variables via `terraform.tfvars`**, not ad hoc `-var` flags; command-line values are ephemeral and easy to forget.
- **Commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`** so provider selection changes are reviewed.

Module style from the [general guidance](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/general-style-structure): start with `main.tf`, include a `README.md`, put examples under `examples/`, declare variables in `variables.tf` with types and descriptions, name numeric variables with units (`ram_size_gb`), give environment-specific variables such as `project_id` no default, and expose useful outputs in `outputs.tf`. Adding a variable with a default is backward compatible; removing one is not. Parameterize only what must vary.

## Core workflow and CI/CD

1. `terraform init` downloads providers and configures the backend.
2. `terraform plan` produces the proposed diff; review it.
3. `terraform apply` makes the changes, acquiring a state lock.
4. `terraform destroy` removes managed resources.

Google's [GitOps tutorial](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/resource-management/managing-infrastructure-as-code) shows the canonical automation shape. Pushes to environment branches (`dev`, `prod`) trigger Cloud Build to **apply**; pushes to any other branch run **plan only** and post the plan on the pull request for review. Changes are merged to `dev`, tested, then merged to `prod`. The tutorial grants project Editor to the build identity only for simplicity and says to use narrower permissions in production, which leads directly to the authentication rules below.

## Authentication

The Google provider uses [Application Default Credentials](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/authentication). The right pattern depends on where Terraform runs:

| Where | Recommended credential |
|---|---|
| Engineer workstation | `gcloud auth application-default login` (user) or `--impersonate-service-account` |
| Cloud Shell | The credentials you signed in with |
| Cloud Build or other Google Cloud compute | An attached **user-managed** service account (not the default one), or impersonation of a least-privilege Terraform service account |
| Outside Google Cloud | Workload Identity Federation; avoid key files |

Details: impersonation requires the **Service Account Token Creator** role (`roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`) on the target service account, and the provider's `impersonate_service_account` field lets teams share one sign-in with a different service account per environment. The documentation states that attaching a user-managed service account is the preferred way to provide credentials to ADC for production code on Google Cloud, advises against the default service account because it is highly privileged by default, and says not to grant Owner, Editor, or Viewer in production. In Cloud Build you select the identity with the build's `serviceAccount` field.

## Managed and Kubernetes-native alternatives

| Option | What it is | Choose when |
|---|---|---|
| Terraform CLI in Cloud Build | You run Terraform in your own pipeline | You want full control of the pipeline and state |
| [Infrastructure Manager](https://cloud.google.com/infrastructure-manager/docs/overview) | Managed service that deploys Terraform configurations (from Cloud Storage, Git, or local) as deployments with revisions and previews | You want Google to run Terraform and keep logs, configs, resource lists, and state per revision; it uses Cloud Build under the hood and does not deploy applications |
| [Config Connector](https://cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/overview) | Open-source Kubernetes add-on that manages Google Cloud resources through CRDs | The team already operates everything through Kubernetes manifests and wants RBAC and desired-state reconciliation for cloud resources |

Config Connector reconciles asynchronously using the identity of its own IAM service account, not the identity of the person who applied the manifest; so permission to create Kubernetes objects in a Config Connector namespace effectively grants authority to change cloud resources. Treat Kubernetes RBAC on those namespaces as cloud IAM.

## Policy as code and the legacy Deployment Manager

**Policy validation** shifts governance left: check the Terraform *plan* against organization rules before apply. [`gcloud beta terraform vet`](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/policy-validation) runs in the pipeline, pulls project data through Google Cloud APIs so the check reflects reality, and evaluates **Terraform constraints** (resource configuration) and **CAI constraints** (Cloud Asset Inventory data). Violations produce warnings or halt the deployment. It is documented as Preview, and it replaces the older `terraform-validator`. In-cluster, Policy Controller (Open Policy Agent based) does the equivalent for Kubernetes resources. Choose policy-as-code in CI when the requirement is "block non-compliant infrastructure before it exists"; Organization Policy and IAM still enforce at runtime, so use both. Third-party tools such as Sentinel or OPA fill the same role for teams standardized on them.

**Deployment Manager** is Google's older IaC service (YAML or Jinja/Python templates). Per its [deprecation notice](https://cloud.google.com/deployment-manager/docs/deprecations), it is no longer supported (support ended in spring 2026), new users have been blocked since June 30, 2026, and the service is scheduled for turn-down after June 30, 2027. Google directs users to Infrastructure Manager, and the **DM Convert** tool turns Deployment Manager configurations into Terraform (some concepts do not convert; use Terraform import for existing resources). Never choose Deployment Manager for new work; if a scenario already uses it, the answer is to migrate to Terraform with Infrastructure Manager.

## Testing and validating infrastructure

Follow the cheapest-first order from Google's [testing guidance](https://cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/best-practices/testing): `terraform validate` and linters, then per-module integration tests in an isolated environment, then full end-to-end deployments. Randomize names and use a fresh project or folder for each test run.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Local state or state committed to Git.** No locking, plaintext secrets, and each machine has a different view of the world.
- **One giant state for everything.** Slow refreshes and a huge blast radius; split by application and environment, and stay well under 100 resources per state.
- **Multiple workspaces on a single backend as the environment separator.** Google recommends separate environment directories with their own state.
- **Hardcoded project IDs, credentials, or tokens in `.tf` files.** Use variables, `terraform.tfvars`, and ADC.
- **Service account key files in the repo or CI variables.** Use attached identities or impersonation.
- **Applying in production without reviewing a plan.** Make `plan` a reviewable CI step and gate `apply`.
- **Granting the pipeline Owner or Editor.** Grant the narrow roles the configuration needs.
- **Unpinned providers and an uncommitted lock file.** Runs stop being deterministic.
- **Manual console edits to managed resources.** They cause drift that the next apply will revert or fight.
- **Starting new infrastructure on Deployment Manager**, or running Terraform with no policy check, so a non-compliant plan reaches apply.
- **Reusing state across tests** or sharing the production project for tests.

## Exam tips

- **Concurrent applies corrupting state: Cloud Storage backend.** The `gcs` backend provides state locking; enable Object Versioning for recovery. Committing state to Git is always wrong.
- **Reuse across environments: modules plus per-environment state.** Modules with input variables, and separate state or directories per environment, are the two recommended practices.
- **Terraform in Cloud Build authenticates through ADC.** Use the build's service account or an impersonated least-privilege one; never a committed key, a hardcoded token, or a personal user token.
- **Plan before apply, gate apply.** Non-environment branches run plan only; environment branches apply after review.
- **Keep each state small.** Google's guideline is no more than 100 resources per state, ideally a few dozen.
- **Prefer the default workspace and separate directories** over many workspaces on a shared backend.
- **Block non-compliant infrastructure before apply with policy validation in CI** (`gcloud beta terraform vet` against the plan). Deployment Manager is legacy and unsupported; the migration path is Terraform and Infrastructure Manager.
- **Managed Terraform is Infrastructure Manager.** If the question wants Google to run Terraform with revisions and previews, choose it; if it wants Kubernetes-style resource management, choose Config Connector.
- **Never use the default service account or Owner/Editor for automation.** Attach a dedicated user-managed service account with least-privilege roles.
